title: SegWay: A simple framework for unsupervised sleep segmentation in experimental EEG recordings
author: Yaghouby, Sunderam

steps.title: Implant EEG/EMG headmount
steps.instruction: Under isoflurane anesthesia, stereotaxically implant a Pinnacle Tech. headmount on each C57BL/6J mouse (8–10 weeks old, 24–29 g, n = 18) using four skull screws: two epidural EEG electrodes (one frontal, one parietal) and two for reference and ground; place the frontal screws 3.0 mm anterior to bregma and insert two silver wires from the headmount rear into the nuchal muscle for bipolar EMG.

steps.title: Recover and prepare recording cage
steps.instruction: Allow mice to recover for about two weeks, then house each in a 7 in × 7 in plexiglass cage with bedding, food and water ad libitum.

steps.title: Connect recording hardware
steps.instruction: Clip a 100× preamplifier to the headmount, route signals through a slip‑ring commutator to a Pinnacle biosignal amplifier, apply a second 50× gain, band‑pass filter EEG (0.5–100 Hz) and EMG (10–100 Hz), sample at 400 Hz with 16‑bit resolution, and store data on a computer; simultaneously record time‑stamped infrared video with a webcam.

steps.title: Acquire 24‑h EEG/EMG recordings
steps.instruction: Record continuous EEG and EMG for 24 h (7 a.m.–9 p.m. Light, 9 p.m.–7 a.m. Dark) for each mouse.

steps.title: Manually score epochs and split datasets
steps.instruction: A human rater scores the 24‑h recording in 4‑s epochs as Wake, NREM, or REM using standard criteria (EMG amplitude for Wake vs sleep; delta power 0.5–4 Hz for NREM, theta power 6–9 Hz for REM); store the scores; then split the EEG/EMG recordings and scores into Light (7 a.m.–9 p.m.) and Dark (9 p.m.–7 a.m.) datasets.

steps.title: Extract signal features per epoch
steps.instruction: In MATLAB, for each 4‑s epoch compute: (1) RMS power of EMG after a 3rd‑order Butterworth band‑pass filter 80–100 Hz; (2) ratio of mean‑squared frontal EEG power filtered in delta (0.5–4 Hz) versus theta (6–9 Hz); (3) ratio of mean‑squared frontal EEG power filtered in high‑frequency (9–45 Hz) versus low‑frequency (0.5–9 Hz). Smooth each feature time series with a four‑point (16 s) moving average and apply a logarithmic scaling.

steps.title: Two‑stage k‑means clustering on Light data
steps.instruction: Apply k‑means++ to the RMS EMG feature values from the Light period to create two clusters (Sleep vs Wake). Then apply k‑means++ again to the Sleep cluster using only the delta‑theta power‑ratio feature to split it into REM and NREM clusters. Use a variance criterion (ratio of within‑cluster distance to mean inter‑centroid distance) and iterate until convergence; the final centroids define the three vigilance states.

steps.title: Classify Light and Dark epochs
steps.instruction: Assign each Light‑period epoch to the nearest of the three centroids obtained above. For the Dark‑period data, assign each epoch to the nearest centroid in the same feature space to obtain out‑of‑sample classifications.

steps.title: Fit hidden Markov model
steps.instruction: First discretize the feature space by running k‑means with a candidate number of clusters between 3 and 15; select the smallest M for which the variance criterion exceeds 90 %. Treat each of the M centroids as a symbolic observation. Compute (a) the discrete conditional probability distribution of each centroid given each of the three vigilance states using the clustered data, and (b) the 3 × 3 state‑transition matrix from the relative frequencies of transitions between the three k‑means‑derived vigilance states. Combine (a) and (b) to form the initial HMM parameters, then optionally refine them with the Baum–Welch EM algorithm to maximum‑likelihood.

steps.title: Decode state sequence with Viterbi
steps.instruction: Apply the Viterbi algorithm to the full time series of log‑scaled, smoothed features using the estimated HMM (refined or initial) to obtain the most probable sequence of vigilance states for both Light and Dark datasets; report the resulting accuracies (≈90 % for Light, ≈91 % for Dark) and note the reduction of spurious brief state transitions.
